definition: Felting is the irreversible matting of wool and other animal fibers into a dense, entangled mass under moisture, warmth and agitation, used to make felt directly from loose fiber.
explanation: Wet felting starts from layers of loose fiber, usually laid in crossing directions. The fiber is wetted with warm soapy water and rubbed, rolled or pressed. Individual fibers creep toward their root ends, work between their neighbors and lock together; as agitation continues, the mass shrinks and firms into a coherent fabric with no yarns at all. Needle felting achieves entanglement dry, with barbed needles, and many industrial 'felts' are synthetic nonwovens made by needlepunching rather than true felting.
example: A hat maker lays two thin, crossing layers of merino fiber, wets them with warm soapy water and rolls the bundle in a mat. At first fibers lift off easily; after several rounds of rolling the layer holds together as one piece and has shrunk visibly. Further throwing and kneading, which is fulling, produces a firm felt that can be shaped over a block.
caution: Felting ability varies: wool with pronounced scales and crimp felts readily, some hair fibers felt poorly, and plant and synthetic fibers do not wet felt at all. Superwash and other shrink-resist treatments are designed to stop felting. Retail 'felt' may be a needlepunched synthetic nonwoven with no scale-driven entanglement and quite different durability.
deeper: The accepted mechanism is the directional frictional effect: friction is lower when a fiber slides root first, with the scales, than tip first, against them, because the scale edges point toward the tip. Cyclic compression and release during agitation therefore produces net migration of each fiber toward its root, a ratchet action that tangles the mass. Water and warmth soften the fiber and increase its extensibility and recovery, and alkaline or acid conditions intensify the effect, while crimp and elastic recovery pull the entangled mass tighter. Because scales drive the effect, chlorination and polymer coatings that smooth or mask them are the basis of shrink-resist finishing.
origins: Wet felting needs no spinning or weaving, only fiber, water, soap and agitation, so it appears in many craft traditions and was long important for rugs, tents and garments among herding peoples. In Europe and North America it underpinned the hat trade. Fur for hat felts was treated with mercury compounds, a step called carroting, and a New Jersey physician described mercurialism in hatters in 1860. A historical review found the hazard was curbed only in 1941, when mercury was diverted to wartime detonators, and argued that the 'mad hatter' image owed more to popular perception than to medical findings.

definition: The shedding of short fiber pieces from textiles during manufacture, wear, washing and drying, measured as the mass, count or length of fragments released.
explanation: Any staple or filament textile can lose short fragments when fibers break or work loose under abrasion and wet agitation. Laundering is the most studied pathway because fragments pass into wastewater, where treatment plants may not retain them all, but drying, wear and production also release them. The phrase fiber fragment avoids confusion with microfiber, which also names deliberately ultrafine fibers, and reflects that natural and regenerated fibers shed too; environmental surveys often report more natural and cellulosic fibers than synthetic ones, although synthetic fragments are the focus of microplastic concern.
example: A student compares two polyester fleece fabrics in a laboratory wash test. One has a brushed surface and loose yarn ends at cut edges; the other is a tightly constructed, unbrushed knit with sealed edges. After several simulated washes with procedural blanks, the filters from the first fabric hold more fragments by mass. The student should repeat the test before concluding which feature caused the difference.
caution: A low result in one test is not a lifetime prediction: release usually falls over successive washes and depends on temperature, load, detergent and machine. Small laboratory devices release more fibers than domestic washing machines, so their results should not be scaled into environmental estimates. Mass and count results are not interchangeable, and recycled polyester sheds synthetic polymer just as virgin polyester does.
deeper: ISO 4484-1:2023 describes laboratory washing in which effluent is filtered and released material is determined gravimetrically; one study using it reported about 0.6 g of fragments per kilogram of warp-knitted polyester per cycle. Counts and length distributions complement mass. A systematic review found that 81% of studies failed to demonstrate clearly the effects they attributed to textile characteristics, so claims about twist, brushing or structure deserve scrutiny. Finishes can matter: plasma-assisted chitosan treatment cut fragment counts from polyester by about 40 to 63% in one test. In cotton and elastane knits, the elastane share of released fibers rose with repeated washing. Capture devices vary widely; one external washing-machine filter caught about 87% of fibers by count, a laundry ball about 26%.
origins: Concern crystallized after a 2011 study found microplastic on shorelines at 18 sites across six continents, with polyester and acrylic fibers resembling those in sewage, and counted more than 1,900 fibers released from a single garment in one wash. Research on laundering, wastewater treatment and filters followed. Standards bodies later published laboratory methods, including ISO 4484-1 in 2023, and France introduced regulation aimed at reducing microfiber release from laundering.
